expected_evidence: Geological: systematic re-sampling of Younger Dryas boundary (YDB) stratigraphic layers across multiple North American sites showing iridium concentrations at or near background crustal levels rather than the enriched spikes originally reported.
Geological: platinum/iridium and platinum-group-element ratios inconsistent with an extraterrestrial (chondritic) source, instead matching terrestrial/volcanic or reworked sediment signatures.
Material: failed independent replication of purported impact markers (magnetic spherules, nanodiamonds, carbon spherules) in YDB sediments by labs unaffiliated with the original proponents.
Material: identification of contamination, misidentification, or non-impact origins (e.g., fungal/algal carbon structures mistaken for nanodiamonds) in re-examined samples.

Astronomical: orbital-mechanics modeling of the Taurid meteor/debris stream showing that a coherent, continent-scale multi-fragment impact swarm at ~10,950 BCE is dynamically implausible or has too low a probability given stream dispersion and Earth-crossing geometry.
Astronomical: absence of a dated, dateable impact crater or crater field in North America correlating to the proposed event.

Model_prior: peer-reviewed critical literature (multiple independent research groups) converging on rejection of the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis as originally formulated, published in the decades following the initial claim.
response.rationale: The interval (-10950) places this at the Younger Dryas onset boundary. Since the hypothesis is a 'refutation' claim, the relevant evidence is not ancient artifacts but modern geological re-sampling of YD boundary sediments, platinum-group-element geochemistry, spherule/nanodiamond replication studies, and astronomical dynamical modeling of the Taurid stream. Per the detectability table for 'younger-dryas': geological=0.65 and astronomical=0.7 are comparatively high, reflecting that sediment cores and stratigraphic layers from ~13,000 years ago are well-studied and widely sampled across North America, and orbital/astronomical modeling does not depend on fragile physical preservation at all (it uses present-day computed dynamics), so it is highly detectable in principle. Material evidence (spherules, nanodiamonds) is lower (0.35) since microscopic markers are harder to unambiguously attribute and are subject to contamination/lab-to-lab variability, which is itself part of why the refutation debate persists. Model_prior is weighted lowest (0.3) since it reflects unverified recall rather than the evidence record itself. Given moderate-to-high detectability for the two dominant evidence classes (geological, astronomical), an absence of unambiguous confirming iridium anomalies is NOT primarily attributable to poor preservation or low detectability — the record is good enough that repeated independent studies could and (per model-prior, unverified) reportedly did fail to replicate the original iridium/impact-marker signal. This supports treating a 'refuted' status as plausible and well-evidenced rather than as a false negative from poor detectability. I set the combined adjustment at 0.55, roughly averaging the four relevant kinds (geological 0.65, astronomical 0.7, material 0.35, model_prior 0.3) with extra weight toward the two higher, more diagnostic channels.
